drawn.name: userName
drawn.description: Unique identifier for the User, typically used by the user to directly authenticate to the service provider. Each User MUST include a non-empty userName value. This identifier MUST be unique across the service provider's entire set of Users. REQUIRED.

drawn.name: name
drawn.description: The components of the user's real name. Providers MAY return just the full name as a single string in the formatted sub-attribute, or they MAY return just the individual component attributes using the other sub-attributes, or they MAY return both. If both variants are returned, they SHOULD be describing the same name, with the formatted name indicating how the component attributes should be combined.

drawn.name: formatted
drawn.description: The full name, including all middle names, titles, and suffixes as appropriate, formatted for display (e.g. 'Ms. Barbara J Jensen, III').

drawn.name: familyName
drawn.description: The family name of the User, or last name in most Western languages (e.g. 'Jensen' given the full name 'Ms. Barbara J Jensen, III').

drawn.name: givenName
drawn.description: The given name of the User, or first name in most Western languages (e.g. 'Barbara' given the full name 'Ms. Barbara J Jensen, III').

drawn.name: honorificPrefix
drawn.description: The honorific prefix(es) of the User, or title in most Western languages (e.g. 'Ms.' given the full name 'Ms. Barbara J Jensen, III').

drawn.name: displayName
drawn.description: The name of the User, suitable for display to end-users. The name SHOULD be the full name of the User being described, if known.

drawn.name: profileUrl
drawn.description: A fully qualified URL pointing to a page representing the User's online profile.

drawn.name: title
drawn.description: The user's title, such as 'Vice President'.

drawn.name: userType
drawn.description: Used to identify the relationship between the organization and the user. Typical values used might be 'Contractor', 'Employee', 'Intern', 'Temp', 'External', and 'Unknown', but any value may be used.

drawn.name: preferredLanguage
drawn.description: Indicates the User's preferred written or spoken language. Generally used for selecting a localized user interface; e.g. 'en_US' specifies the language English and country US.

drawn.name: active
drawn.description: A Boolean value indicating the User's administrative status.

drawn.name: password
drawn.description: The User's cleartext password. This attribute is intended to be used as a means to specify an initial password when creating a new User or to reset an existing User's password.

drawn.name: emails
drawn.description: Email addresses for the user. The value SHOULD be canonicalized by the service provider, e.g. 'bjensen@example.com' instead of 'bjensen@EXAMPLE.COM'. Canonical type values of 'work', 'home', and 'other'.

drawn.name: value
drawn.description: Email addresses for the user. The value SHOULD be canonicalized by the service provider, e.g. 'bjensen@example.com' instead of 'bjensen@EXAMPLE.COM'. Canonical type values of 'work', 'home', and 'other'.

drawn.name: type
drawn.description: A label indicating the attribute's function, e.g. 'work' or 'home'.

drawn.name: phoneNumbers
drawn.description: Phone numbers for the User. The value SHOULD be canonicalized by the service provider according to the format specified in RFC 3966, e.g. 'tel:+1-201-555-0123'. Canonical type values of 'work', 'home', 'mobile', 'fax', 'pager', and 'other'.

drawn.name: value
drawn.description: Phone number of the User.

drawn.name: type
drawn.description: A label indicating the attribute's function, e.g. 'work', 'home', 'mobile'.

drawn.name: addresses
drawn.description: A physical mailing address for this User. Canonical type values of 'work', 'home', and 'other'. This attribute is a complex type with the following sub-attributes.

drawn.name: formatted
drawn.description: The full mailing address, formatted for display or use with a mailing label. This attribute MAY contain newlines.

drawn.name: streetAddress
drawn.description: The full street address component, which may include house number, street name, P.O. box, and multi-line extended street address information. This attribute MAY contain newlines.

drawn.name: locality
drawn.description: The city or locality component.

drawn.name: region
drawn.description: The state or region component.

drawn.name: postalCode
drawn.description: The zip code or postal code component.

drawn.name: country
drawn.description: The country name component.

drawn.name: type
drawn.description: A label indicating the attribute's function, e.g. 'work' or 'home'.

drawn.name: groups
drawn.description: A list of groups to which the user belongs, either through direct membership, through nested groups, or dynamically calculated.

drawn.name: value
drawn.description: The identifier of the User's group.

drawn.name: $ref
drawn.description: The URI of the corresponding 'Group' resource to which the user belongs.

drawn.name: display
drawn.description: A human-readable name, primarily used for display purposes. READ-ONLY.

drawn.name: type
drawn.description: A label indicating the attribute's function, e.g. 'direct' or 'indirect'.

drawn.name: displayName
drawn.description: A human-readable name for the Group. REQUIRED.

drawn.name: value

drawn.name: type

drawn.name: organization

drawn.name: division

drawn.name: department

NOT SENT: unchanged, so a provisioning client that knows nothing of this extension cannot unlink anybody by leaving it out. Sent, even empty: replaced, and every link removed ends the sessions that partner signed the person in to. A link another person carries is refused 409.

READ-ONLY, as RFC 7643 section 4.1.2 requires. Membership is a fact about the GROUP's entry, so it is changed through a Group resource and never through a User one. Resolved by ldap_server.js's groupsOfUser(), which is the same function the groups claim reads — so a token and a SCIM resource cannot disagree about who is in what.

group.note: READ resolves member, uniqueMember and memberUid alike; WRITE puts a new value in `member`, since a SCIM member id is a DN. A dangling member — a DN nothing is stored at — is returned as a member, because the group saying so is the fact, and this directory does no referential integrity on purpose.

authenticationSchemes.name: OAuth 2.0 Bearer Token
authenticationSchemes.description: An access token issued by this service's own authorization server, presented as "Authorization: Bearer <token>". Any grant will do — authorization code, client credentials, password, refresh, device, token exchange — but the SCIM scopes are issued only to a client whose oauthAllowedScope declares them, in every mode. The token must carry the read scope to read and the write scope to write, its client must still declare that scope, it must be one THIS service signed, must not have been revoked, and must not have been narrowed by RFC 8707 to a different resource.

authenticationSchemes.name: OAuth 2.0 DPoP (proof-of-possession) token
authenticationSchemes.description: The proof-of-possession token RFC 7644 section 2 names, in the shape this service already issues: an access token bound to a key (cnf.jkt), presented as "Authorization: DPoP <token>" with a fresh DPoP proof over the method and URL. An RFC 8705 certificate-bound token is the other proof-of-possession form and is honoured on the same path. Handled by the same check as the Bearer row — they are one credential with two ways of being held — and listed separately because a client reading this document is entitled to know the bound form is understood.

authenticationSchemes.name: HTTP Basic
authenticationSchemes.description: In product mode the password is verified against the person's hashed userPassword, and a person who holds or must hold a second factor is refused their own password and uses an app password. In development mode any username and any password pass, exactly as every LDAP bind there succeeds — with the single exception of the password "invalid", which is refused so that a 401 stays reachable — so what this authenticates there is a NAME, and that name is what the audit log records. RFC 7644 section 2 DISCOURAGES this scheme, in those words, because it rests on a relatively static symmetric secret; it is implemented anyway because it is what a provisioning client most often meets and its 401 handling is worth being able to run.

authenticationSchemes.name: HTTP Digest
authenticationSchemes.description: In product mode this scheme is NOT offered, and is refused: a password is stored as a salted scrypt hash, which cannot answer an RFC 7616 exchange. In development mode it is the one scheme where the password really is checked, and it cannot not be: the response is a hash over the password, so a server that accepted anything would not be performing the exchange at all. So it does what Kerberos does for the same reason — ANY username authenticates and every one of them shares one password (scim.digestPassword). SHA-256 and SHA-512-256 are offered, in that order, with the -sess variants, and MD5 last only where scim.digestMd5 turns it on; qop is auth. A wrong password is a 401, a stale nonce is a 401 with stale=true, and a replayed nonce count is a 401 — three negatives that are otherwise hard to provoke.

authenticationSchemes.name: HOBA (HTTP Origin-Bound Authentication)
authenticationSchemes.description: The signature-based scheme RFC 7644 section 2 names, and the only one of the six with no password anywhere in it. A client registers a public key at /.well-known/hoba/register — in development mode anybody may, for any name; in product mode only the signed-in owner of an existing account may, and a registration never creates an account — and then signs the server's challenge together with the origin, the realm and its own key id and nonce. THE SIGNATURE IS REALLY VERIFIED, in both modes: a signature check that passes anything is not the scheme. RSA with SHA-256 (algorithm 0) only.

authenticationSchemes.name: Session cookie
authenticationSchemes.description: The browser sign-on session this service already has — the one /authn/login establishes and WS-Federation shares — offered here because section 2 names it: "clients may assert HTTP cookies over TLS that contain an authentication state understood by the SCIM service provider". It is what makes a SCIM call from a page on this service work with no second credential. There is no challenge for it: a server cannot ask for a cookie in WWW-Authenticate, so it is used when it is there and never demanded.

authenticationSchemes.name: TLS client certificate
authenticationSchemes.description: Mutual TLS, the first scheme RFC 7644 section 2 names. Available only where this request arrived over TLS with a certificate that VERIFIED against an anchor in the client truststore (/admin/tls/trust) — so on the main port only when it is bound as HTTPS (global.https, which oauth2.rfc9700 turns on). A certificate from an outside certificate authority (an anchor somebody added) is the person or application whose entry stores it, byte for byte, in userCertificate, and nothing else: stored on no entry or on several, it is not this credential. A person's certificate this realm issued is filed under its subject in RFC 4514 form. It is not recorded again here: tls_server.js records a certificate once per CONNECTION on purpose, and counting it per request would undo that from the other end. A certificate this realm issued to an APPLICATION is that application, and may do only what its oauthAllowedScope declares: the read scope to read and the write scope to write, asked on every request, so one that declares neither is refused. A person's certificate, issued here or stored on their entry, may do both.

body.name: IyaStsUser
body.description: This service's own User extension: which federation partners' subjects are linked to the person, and the Identity Assurance claims no standard schema carries (#128).

attributes.name: salutation
attributes.description: A formal salutation, e.g. "Ms" (the Claims Registration's salutation).

attributes.name: birthFamilyName
attributes.description: The family name at birth.

attributes.name: birthGivenName
attributes.description: The given name at birth.

attributes.name: birthMiddleName
attributes.description: The middle name at birth.

attributes.name: alsoKnownAs
attributes.description: Another name the person is known by, e.g. a stage name.

attributes.name: placeOfBirthCountry
attributes.description: The country of birth, ISO 3166-1 alpha-2.

attributes.name: placeOfBirthRegion
attributes.description: The region of birth.

attributes.name: placeOfBirthLocality
attributes.description: The locality of birth.

attributes.name: homeCell
attributes.description: On a create in a service deployed as several regions: the region the person is homed in, whose data stays there. The realm's default when not sent. Never returned, and not changed by a later write.

attributes.name: federationLinks
attributes.description: Each a federation partner's identifier for the person, through one service-provider-side relationship. Not sent: unchanged. Sent: replaced; a link removed ends the sessions that partner signed the person in to.

subAttributes.name: relationship
subAttributes.description: The service-provider-side relationship.

subAttributes.name: issuer
subAttributes.description: The partner's entity ID or iss; the relationship's fedPeer when omitted.

subAttributes.name: subject
subAttributes.description: The partner's stable identifier for the person (an OpenID Connect sub, a SAML persistent NameID).

body.name: CustomAttributes
body.description: This realm's custom attributes, as its administrators define them on Directory → Policies → Attribute policy. Each realm has its own; not sent on a PUT, they are left as they are.
